title: The origins of artificial intelligence
matchup: McCarthy and the Dartmouth project (1955–1956) vs earlier automata, cybernetics and computation theory
question: Is treating Dartmouth 1956 as the birth of AI historically misleading given the earlier work and meetings cited by Schmidhuber?

usual_credit.summary: John McCarthy is conventionally credited with the artificial-intelligence label and, with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon, the Dartmouth research project that helped establish a named field. [Dartmouth's institutional history](https://home.dartmouth.edu/about/artificial-intelligence-ai-coined-dartmouth) calls the 1956 gathering the birth of the field, while the original proposal is dated 31 August 1955. That proposal itself discusses earlier neural-network research and existing computing work, so founding a research community need not mean inventing every technique that later falls within it.

works.who: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon
works.title: A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence

claim.summary: Schmidhuber argues that both practical and theoretical work now called AI existed before Dartmouth, citing Torres y Quevedo's chess automaton, Gödel's results and cybernetics. He also points to the 1951 Paris meeting on calculating machines and human thought as an earlier AI conference. His stronger formulation describes the 1956 naming as a renaming of cybernetics and argues that today's neural methods are closer to that older tradition than to the symbolic work often associated with Dartmouth.

response.summary: No point-by-point public reply from Dartmouth's organizers to Schmidhuber's renaming claim was located in the sources reviewed. Historian David C. Brock's [account of the Paris meeting](https://spectrum.ieee.org/cybernetics-computer-design-and-a-meeting-of-the-minds) supports its importance but says calling it an AI birthplace depends on how the term is defined, rather than presenting one uncontested starting date. The original Dartmouth proposal also includes a section on neuron nets and acknowledges earlier researchers, which complicates a description of its organizers as merely renaming a single older field. In the public [Connectionists discussion](https://mailman.srv.cs.cmu.edu/pipermail/connectionists/2023-January/039184.html), Gary Marcus and Andreas Wichert separately challenged Schmidhuber's history for giving too little attention to symbolic AI; that was a criticism of its balance, not a denial that earlier automata and cybernetics existed.

quotes.text: This view hinges on just how one takes the phrase “artificial intelligence.”

agreed_facts: The Dartmouth proposal is dated 31 August 1955 and proposes research for summer 1956: http://www-formal.stanford.edu/jmc/history/dartmouth/dartmouth.html
The proposal includes a section headed Neuron Nets and names earlier researchers: http://www-formal.stanford.edu/jmc/history/dartmouth/dartmouth.html
The Paris meeting on calculating machines and human thought took place in January 1951: https://www.computerhistory.org/collections/catalog/102805935
Brock documents cybernetic machines and a Torres y Quevedo chess-machine demonstration at that Paris meeting: https://spectrum.ieee.org/cybernetics-computer-design-and-a-meeting-of-the-minds
crux: The dispute turns on whether founding AI means the earliest machine behavior now classed as intelligent, mathematical foundations relevant to intelligence, or formation of the named research field. Earlier examples establish antecedents, but deciding whether Dartmouth was merely a renaming also requires examining the aims and boundaries of the communities involved.
